dock.readingCaveat: What counts as healthy moves with the crop and its growth stage — read a value against where this block is in its season, not on its own.

def.ndvi: Compares near-infrared reflectance with red: (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red). Healthy leaves reflect infrared strongly and absorb red, so the value rises with how much living, photosynthesising canopy covers the ground.
def.evi: A vigour index built to survive what breaks NDVI: it uses the blue band to cancel haze and aerosol, and a soil term to damp the background. It keeps separating dense canopies apart after NDVI has flattened near its ceiling.
def.savi: NDVI with a soil-brightness correction folded in (L = 0.5). Bare ground between rows inflates a plain NDVI reading, so SAVI is the more honest measure of vigour while cover is still patchy — early season, wide rows, or a thin stand.
def.ndre: Compares near-infrared with the red-edge band, the narrow slice where chlorophyll absorption starts to fall away. It tracks chlorophyll — and so nitrogen — deeper into the canopy than NDVI, and keeps responding at full cover once NDVI has saturated.
def.gndvi: NDVI with green in place of red: (NIR − Green) / (NIR + Green). Green reflectance is governed by chlorophyll concentration, so this leans towards leaf greenness and nitrogen rather than towards sheer canopy size.
def.ndwi: McFeeters' surface-water index, (Green − NIR) / (Green + NIR). Water reflects green and absorbs infrared, so open water sits above zero while canopy and dry soil stay negative. It finds standing water on the block — not moisture inside the leaves.
def.ndmi: Compares near-infrared with shortwave infrared: (NIR − SWIR1) / (NIR + SWIR1). Leaf water absorbs shortwave infrared, so the value falls as tissue dries — usually days before the canopy visibly wilts or NDVI reacts.

scale.ndvi: Runs −1 to 1. Below 0.2 is effectively bare; 0.2–0.6 is a developing canopy; 0.6 and above is dense and actively growing.
scale.evi: Runs −1 to 1, and over crops usually 0.1–0.8. Below 0.2 is near-bare; 0.2–0.55 is developing; above 0.55 is dense cover.
scale.savi: Reads on roughly the same 0–1 scale as NDVI. Below 0.2 is near-bare; 0.2–0.55 developing; above 0.55 dense. Expect it to sit below NDVI wherever soil still shows.
scale.ndre: Over crops it usually runs 0.1–0.6. Below 0.2 is a thin or nitrogen-short canopy; 0.3–0.45 is comfortable; above 0.45 is well fed.
scale.gndvi: Usually 0.1–0.7 over crops. Below 0.2 is near-bare; 0.35–0.55 is a healthy green canopy; above 0.55 is dense and chlorophyll-rich.
scale.ndwi: Runs −1 to 1, and the scale is inverted against the canopy indices: a healthy crop reads well below −0.15, and anything above 0 is standing water.
scale.ndmi: Runs −1 to 1. Below 0.2 is a dry, stressed canopy; 0.2–0.4 is moderate; 0.4–0.6 is well watered; above 0.6 is a very wet canopy.

ndvi.bare: Bare soil, water or cloud — there is effectively no living canopy here.
ndvi.verySparse: Almost no green cover. Normal before emergence; a failed or removed stand if this block should be in crop.
ndvi.sparse: Sparse canopy. Expected soon after planting, and low for a crop that should be in full growth.
ndvi.developing: Canopy is filling in and partly covering the ground. On track mid-season, behind at peak.
ndvi.dense: Dense, actively growing canopy — the healthy range for most crops at full cover.
ndvi.veryDense: Very dense canopy. NDVI flattens out up here, so use NDRE to tell a good canopy from an excellent one.

evi.sparse: Sparse canopy — early growth, or a thin stand for this point in the season.
evi.developing: Canopy is developing, with soil still showing between plants.
evi.dense: Dense, vigorous canopy — a healthy reading at full cover.
evi.veryDense: Very high biomass. EVI still resolves detail up here, where NDVI would have flattened.

savi.bare: Bare ground — the soil correction leaves almost nothing behind.
savi.verySparse: Barely any canopy above the soil background.
savi.sparse: Sparse cover. This is the reading to trust over NDVI while so much soil is visible.
savi.developing: Canopy developing over partly visible soil.
savi.dense: Dense canopy — vigorous once the soil background is corrected out.
savi.veryDense: Very dense canopy; the soil correction barely changes the answer at this much cover.

ndre.bare: No meaningful red-edge signal — bare ground, or a canopy that has senesced.
ndre.low: Low chlorophyll. A young canopy, a crop shutting down for harvest, or a real nitrogen shortfall.
ndre.moderate: Moderate chlorophyll. Worth a tissue or soil-nitrogen check if the crop is past early growth.
ndre.good: Healthy chlorophyll and nitrogen status for most crops at full cover.
ndre.high: Strong red-edge signal — a well-fed, chlorophyll-rich canopy.

gndvi.low: Little green biomass — early growth, senescence, or a chlorophyll shortfall.
gndvi.moderate: Moderate greenness. Reasonable while the canopy is still closing.
gndvi.good: Healthy green canopy with good chlorophyll content.

ndwi.denseCanopy: Strongly negative — a dense canopy with no standing water. This is where a healthy field sits.
ndwi.vegetated: Vegetated ground with no surface water.
ndwi.bareOrDamp: Close to the water threshold. Usually bare or lightly covered soil, but wet ground reads the same — check NDVI to tell them apart.
ndwi.standingWater: Above zero: open water on the block. Expected during and just after flood irrigation; otherwise it points at ponding or poor drainage.
ndwi.openWater: Open water over much of the block — standing flood water, or a pond or canal inside the boundary.

ndmi.bare: Too little canopy to read moisture from — this is bare ground, not a dry crop.
ndmi.severeStress: Very dry canopy. Severe water stress, or a stand too sparse to hold moisture.
ndmi.stress: Dry canopy — moderate to high water stress for a crop at full cover. Check the irrigation schedule.
ndmi.moderate: Moderate canopy moisture. Comfortable while cover is still partial, on the dry side at full canopy.
ndmi.wellWatered: Well-watered canopy with no sign of moisture stress.
ndmi.veryWet: Very high canopy water content — a full, well-irrigated canopy. If it stays here, check drainage.
